title: Grill — Harness account stacks (backup accounts, automatic failover)
summary:
The investigation proved the hard part is real: a backup account can inherit the **conversation** for Claude, Codex and OpenCode, but user-level **MCP servers, skills, commands and settings are per account** today, and only three kinds have live quota. This round settles the **10 decisions that change the plan's shape** plus **5 defaults** I would bet on. Start with the blocking questions in **The stack model** and **When the swap happens**; the confirm list at the end is one click each.

Source: `docs/plans/harness-account-stacks-investigation.md` (step 1). There is no PRD outside this repo; the plan written from these answers becomes the binding spec.

proven.text: **Claude Code can resume another account's transcript.** With `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=<backup>`, a transcript copied into `<backup>/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<sid>.jsonl`, and `claude --resume <sid>`, the model received the prior conversation and the backup's transcript grew in place. A bogus path printed `No conversation found with session ID`.

evidence.label: S1 verdict

proven.text: **Codex can resume a copied rollout.** A `rollout-…-<uuid>.jsonl` copied into a fresh `CODEX_HOME/sessions/…` made `codex exec resume <uuid>` emit `thread.started` with the same id. An unknown id failed with `no rollout found for thread id`.

evidence.label: S2 verdict

proven.text: **OpenCode can move a session, but not merge it.** `opencode session export` + `import --standalone` preserved the same `ses_…` id and 78 messages in a fresh XDG home; a second import said `Session already exists`. Child sessions are not included.

evidence.label: S3 verdict

proven.text: **The other five kinds are unproven.** Cursor may be cloud-bound; fx, gemini, copilot and antigravity session copies were not spiked. Including them in v1 needs per-kind proof first.

evidence.label: S4 verdict

proven.text: **User-level capabilities are per account.** Claude reads `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/skills` and `.claude.json`; cursor/fx/opencode read `<HOME>`; codex reads `CODEX_HOME`; copilot reads `$COPILOT_HOME`. Project-level entries are shared because every account runs in the same task worktree.

evidence.label: per-kind user roots
home env mapping

proven.text: **Only three kinds have live quota.** `USAGE_SUPPORTED_KINDS = ["claude-code", "codex", "cursor"]`, polled every 10 minutes; the other five can only be detected reactively.

evidence.label: supported kinds
poll cadence

proven.text: **Today a same-kind alias switch starts fresh.** `findLastSessionIdForHarness` only resumes an id created by the current harness, and `reconcileTaskSession` kills the session on any harness-id change. Stacks are a deliberate exception.

evidence.label: session scoping rule
any id change kills the session

proven.text: **No stack/failover tests exist.** `orchestrator-session-harness.test.ts` pins the opposite behavior; a naive change can pass the suite without proving anything.

evidence.label: S5 verdict

sections.title: The stack model
sections.intro: These decide whether `Task`, `AgentProfile`, pipelines and bundles need a new reference, or whether a stack is just a property of the account.

questions.title: What is a "stack" in the model: a fallback chain attached to each account, or a separate named group?
questions.why: This is the biggest shape decision. It decides whether `Task`, `AgentProfile`, pipeline snapshots and the bundle format need a new field, and whether every picker changes.
questions.context: Today `Task.agent` stores one harness id, an Agent profile stores one `harness`, and a pipeline step creates its task with `agent: profile.harness`. Bundles export a `{id, kind, label}` harness ref, never accounts. An implicit chain needs no new task/profile/pipeline/bundle field and makes profiles and pipelines work automatically. An explicit group allows multiple stacks sharing an account and per-task choice, but touches every picker, PATCH validation, the profile snapshot, the pipeline format and the bundle.

evidence.label: the account row id is what tasks store
pipeline steps bind one account
bundles carry a harness ref, not accounts

options.label: A chain attached to each account
options.description: An account belongs to at most one stack. A task's stack is derived from `Task.agent`; a swap changes `Task.agent` to the next member. No new task/profile/pipeline/bundle field.
options.consequence: Smallest blast radius; profiles, pipelines and bundles work unchanged. Adding a backup applies to every task on that account, and an account cannot be in two stacks.
options.preview:
harness_stacks(id, label, kind)
harness_stack_members(stack_id, harness_id, position)
  UNIQUE(harness_id)   -- one stack per account

Task.agent = "claude-work"  ->  stack [claude-work, claude-backup]

options.label: A named stack selected per task/profile
options.description: A stack is its own entity. A task or Agent profile stores `harnessStackId`; `Task.agent` remains the current member. Multiple stacks can share an account.
options.consequence: Most flexible, but adds `harnessStackId` to tasks, profiles, pipeline snapshots and the bundle, plus a picker on every launch surface and PATCH validation.
options.preview:
harness_stacks(id, label, kind)
harness_stack_members(stack_id, harness_id, position)

Task.harnessStackId = "work-train"
Task.agent           = "claude-work"   -- current member

options.label: Each task stores its own list of accounts
options.description: No global stack entity; a task carries an ordered list of member ids.
options.consequence: Simple for one-off tasks, but every task repeats the configuration and profiles/pipelines need arrays. Probably not worth it.

recommendation.reason: The requirement is a per-account train, and this is the only model where profiles, pipelines and bundles keep working without a format change.

questions.title: Must every member be the same harness kind, or can a stack fall through to a different kind (Claude → Codex)?
questions.why: Model ids, mode/effort semantics, session formats and often the provider change with the kind. Cross-kind would reset the task's model/mode/effort and need a context handoff.
questions.context: The requirement says "same harness". In this repo a harness row has a `kind`; built-in rows' ids equal the kind, and an additional account is an alias of the same kind. Same-kind keeps the task's model/mode/effort valid and makes the provider session transferable. Cross-kind fallback (Claude → Codex) is a different feature.

evidence.label: kind is the identity; aliases share it
a cross-kind switch already resets model/mode/effort
evidence.code:
if (afterKind && beforeKind !== afterKind) {
      const nextMode = defaultModeFor(afterKind);

options.label: Same kind only
options.description: Every member has the same `kind`. A cross-kind fallback is rejected at stack creation.
options.consequence: Model, mode and effort stay valid; session transfer is possible. Matches the requirement's "same harness".

options.label: Allow any kind, with a reset
options.description: A stack can fall through to a different kind; the new run resets model/mode/effort and starts a fresh session.
options.consequence: A separate, much larger design: context handoff, per-kind model defaults, and a visible "fresh session" notice.

options.label: Allow cross-kind only when the model is compatible
options.description: Fall through only if the next kind offers the same model family.
options.consequence: Still needs the cross-kind reset and handoff, plus a compatibility table that will age badly.

recommendation.reason: The requirement says "same harness", and same-kind is the only version where the model/mode/effort and the provider session survive the move.

questions.title: Which harness kinds must a stack support in v1?
questions.why: Only Claude, Codex and OpenCode have a proven session-transfer mechanism. The other five are unproven and may need provider-specific spikes. This decides the size of v1 and whether "seamless" is a promise or a best effort.
questions.context: S1 proved Claude transcript copy + `--resume`. S2 proved Codex rollout copy + `exec resume`. S3 proved OpenCode export/import (a move, not a merge). S4 left cursor, gemini, fx, copilot and antigravity unproven; cursor may be server/cloud-bound. A v1 that silently degrades to a summary for those kinds may not meet "seamless".

evidence.label: S1–S3: transfer proven for claude, codex, opencode
S4: the other five are unproven

options.label: Claude Code only
options.description: The best-supported kind and the most common additional-account case.
options.consequence: Smallest v1; other kinds show "stacks are not supported yet".

options.label: Claude Code + Codex + OpenCode
options.description: Exactly the three kinds with a proven transfer mechanism. Other kinds cannot join a stack in v1 and say so clearly.
options.consequence: No silent degradation. The other five wait for a per-kind adapter and a spike.
options.preview:
Claude    copy transcript -> <backup>/projects/<cwd>/<sid>.jsonl, --resume <sid>
Codex     copy rollout     -> <backup>/.codex/sessions/..., exec resume <id>
OpenCode  export/import    -> same ses_ id, move not merge

options.label: All eight, after five more spikes
options.description: Prove cursor, gemini, fx, copilot and antigravity before planning; then support every kind.
options.consequence: Meets the broadest reading of the requirement, but adds five investigations and five adapters before the plan can start.

options.label: All eight, with a visible context-file fallback
options.description: Proven kinds get exact transfer; the rest start a fresh provider session and receive an Agetor-rendered transcript with a visible "context handoff" notice.
options.consequence: Every kind can fail over, but the unproven ones are token-heavy, cannot preserve partial tool state, and are visibly not seamless.

recommendation.reason: It is the widest scope that can honestly promise "the conversation survives"; a silent fallback for the other five would fail the requirement without telling the user.

questions.title: Claude Code handles a usage limit by waiting for the reset itself. Should Agetor preempt that and swap to the backup?
questions.why: If Agetor does not preempt it, a Claude task can sit idle until the 5-hour reset even with a healthy backup. If it does, Agetor must detect a notice it deliberately ignores today.
questions.context: The driver suppresses Claude's `Usage limit reached · continuing automatically at …` notices; the turn stays in flight and Claude resumes itself at reset. There is no persisted event for it. The quota poller may know the session meter is at 100%, but the turn is already running. This is the difference between "automatic swap when the primary reaches its limit" and "swap only after a hard failure".

evidence.label: Claude's auto-continue notice is deliberately not carded
evidence.code:
/** Usage-limit AUTO-CONTINUE notices, which carry a `MODAL_FOOTER_RE` phrase
 *  (`… · esc to cancel`) but need no user action — claude resumes on its own.
 *  Evidence (2.1.239 binary): `Usage limit reached · continuing automatically
 *  at 8am · esc to cancel`, `… continuing shortly · esc to cancel`, `…
 *  continuing automatically when it resets · esc to cancel`.

evidence.label: quota meters know the reset time

options.label: Detect the notice and swap immediately
options.description: Agetor recognizes Claude's auto-continue notice, stops the turn, transfers the transcript, and continues on the backup.
options.consequence: Delivers the promise for the most-used kind. Needs a new pane/JSONL sentinel and a careful stop/transfer path; the old turn is interrupted at the limit, not at a natural end.
options.preview:
Usage limit reached · continuing automatically at 8am · esc to cancel
        │
        ▼
Agetor stops the turn, copies the transcript to the backup,
resumes with --resume <sid> + a continuation prompt.

options.label: Leave Claude's own wait alone
options.description: Claude keeps its auto-continue behavior; the stack only reacts to a hard API error or an explicit failure.
options.consequence: No new sentinel, but a task can idle for hours with a healthy backup. This does not meet "automatically swap when the primary reaches its limit" for Claude.

options.label: Skip an exhausted account before the turn only
options.description: The quota meter prevents starting on an exhausted member; if the limit hits mid-turn, Claude waits.
options.consequence: No new sentinel, but a mid-turn limit still stalls. Best-effort, not seamless.

recommendation.reason: The feature's promise is that execution keeps running; leaving Claude's built-in wait in place would make the most common account kind the one case where the train does nothing.

sections.title: When the swap happens
sections.intro: These decide what triggers a move, and what happens to the turn that hit the limit.

questions.title: Which failures count as "this account reached its limit" and should trigger a swap?
questions.why: A false swap can duplicate work and burn the backup; a missed swap leaves the task blocked. The classifier is the safety boundary.
questions.context: There is no cross-kind exhaustion concept today. Only Claude, Codex and Cursor have live quota. Claude already turns a synthetic API error into a `blocked` task (reason `api-error`). 5xx/529 are account-independent, so swapping on them just burns the backup. Auth failures are account-specific but are not a limit; the app already has an actionable credential-error panel. A model-scoped meter (e.g. "Opus") is not account-wide.

evidence.label: only three kinds have live quota
evidence.code: export const USAGE_SUPPORTED_KINDS = ["claude-code", "codex", "cursor"] as const satisfies readonly AgentKind[];

evidence.label: a claude API error already blocks the task
evidence.code:
const nextColumn: ColumnId = wasCancelled
            ? "ready"
            : (wasApiError || wasSessionDied || wasUnknownCommand) ? "blocked"
            : newStatus === "succeeded" ? "review" : "ready";

evidence.label: meters are model-scoped, not account-wide
evidence.code:
/** Optional model/window scope this meter applies to (e.g. "Opus", "Sonnet"). */
  scope?: string;

options.label: Provider quota exhausted
options.description: A session/weekly meter at 100%, or a provider usage-limit notice.
options.consequence: The clearest signal; the only one with a known reset time.

options.label: HTTP 429 / rate limited
options.description: A per-account or per-model rate limit.
options.consequence: Good failover signal, but a model-scoped 429 may not mean the account is exhausted.

options.label: 402 / insufficient credits
options.description: Extra usage required or the account is out of credits.
options.consequence: Account-specific and unlikely to clear soon; a good swap signal.

options.label: Auth / login failure
options.description: 401, expired token, "not logged in".
options.consequence: Not a limit. Swapping hides a real problem; block with the credential panel instead.

options.label: Provider outage / 529 / 5xx / network
options.description: The provider is down or the network failed.
options.consequence: Account-independent; swapping just burns the backup on the same outage.

options.label: The task's model is not offered on this account
options.description: The backup has a smaller catalog and cannot run the task's model.
options.consequence: Pre-flight should skip that member, not discover it after a failed turn.

recommendation.reason: These are account-specific and likely to clear with a reset; the excluded three are either not limits or not account-specific.

questions.title: When the limit hits mid-turn, what should happen to the turn?
questions.why: Continuing the same turn can duplicate tool side effects; ending the turn loses the seamless requirement. This is the single biggest behavioral decision.
questions.context: S1–S3 prove the provider session can be transferred, so the backup can resume with the full conversation. But a tool call may have partially executed when the limit hit. Agetor's `run_events` transcript is canonical; the provider session is the model's context. Pending permission cards and background subagents belong to the old session and cannot move.

evidence.label: S1: the transferred transcript is what the model receives
settlement is the natural seam
queued follow-ups are drained after a run settles
evidence.code: async function drainFollowUpQueues(taskId: string, runId: string, wasCancelled: boolean): Promise<void> {

options.label: Resume the same turn on the backup
options.description: Stop the old turn, transfer the provider session, and resume with a synthetic "continue" prompt. If the failure happened before any tool call, retry the original prompt instead. If the transfer fails, block with a clear message rather than silently starting fresh.
options.consequence: Meets the seamless promise for proven kinds. Needs per-kind stop/transfer/resume adapters and a careful guard against re-running a tool call that already has a result.

options.label: Always continue, even after a partial tool call
options.description: Same as above, but never refuse to continue.
options.consequence: Can duplicate a file edit or a command; the user sees the same tool twice. Too risky without per-tool idempotency.

options.label: End the turn, continue on the next message
options.description: Let the turn fail, show the swap notice, and let the next user message run on the backup.
options.consequence: Safest for side effects, but the task visibly stops. Does not meet "execution must keep running".

options.label: Block and ask the user
options.description: Stop the turn, show the notice, and leave the task blocked for a manual Run.
options.consequence: No automatic failover at all; the user must click.

recommendation.reason: It is the only option that both keeps the task running and avoids repeating a tool call that already completed; the "block on transfer failure" clause keeps the fallback honest.

sections.title: What the backup inherits
sections.intro: The conversation is only half of "keep the context". These decide what happens to the provider session, the user-level capabilities and the credentials.

questions.title: What does "preserve the conversation" mean for the backup?
questions.why: The exact provider session preserves tool calls, plan state and partial turns; an Agetor transcript/summary is universal but token-heavy and cannot preserve partial tool state.
questions.context: S1 proved exact Claude transfer: the copied transcript is what the model receives, and the backup writes the updated transcript in place. S2 proved Codex resolves a copied rollout. S3 proved OpenCode export/import preserves the session id and messages but is a move, not a merge. The other five are unproven. Agetor's own transcript is always preserved because the task and its `run_events` stay the same.

evidence.label: S1 detail: copy into the next account's standard path
S3 detail: import is not a merge
session ids are scoped to the creating harness
evidence.code: - **Session ids are scoped to the harness that created them.** Every resume asks `findLastSessionIdForHarness(taskId, column, harnessId)` (`orchestrator.ts`) for its own column on a run of the task's current harness, so a second account of the same kind starts fresh instead of resuming an id its data dir doesn't hold.

options.label: Exact provider session
options.description: Transfer the provider's session state to the backup and resume it. If the transfer fails, block with a clear message; never silently start a fresh session.
options.consequence: Best fidelity and the only option that preserves tool calls and plan state. Per-kind adapters; OpenCode is a move, so switching back needs a delete/import cycle.

options.label: Agetor transcript + fresh session
options.description: Render the task's event log to a transcript, start a fresh provider session, and tell the new agent to read it and continue.
options.consequence: Works for every kind, but token-heavy, loses partial tool state, and is visibly a different conversation.

options.label: Exact where proven, transcript elsewhere
options.description: Use the exact session for the proven kinds and the transcript fallback for the rest, with a visible "context handoff" notice.
options.consequence: Covers more kinds, but is two mechanisms to build and test, and the fallback is not seamless.

recommendation.reason: The requirement is to keep the context, not to summarize it; exact transfer is proven for the v1 kinds, and a clear failure is better than a silent fresh session.

questions.title: How should the backup get the primary's user-level MCP servers, skills, commands and CLI settings?
questions.why: "Must be preserved" cannot be true today without a sharing mechanism: user-level entries live in each account's isolated home. Project-level entries are already shared through the worktree.
questions.context: Claude reads `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/.claude.json` `mcpServers` and `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/skills`; cursor/fx/opencode read `<HOME>`; copilot reads `$COPILOT_HOME`; codex reads `config.toml`. Agetor already discovers these per account. Auto-sharing needs per-kind injection or copies and must exclude credentials and OAuth tokens. Hooks and permission settings are security-sensitive because they execute code.

evidence.label: per-kind user roots
five kinds re-home the whole process

options.label: Each account is configured separately
options.description: No sharing. Agetor compares the members' user-level MCP servers/skills at stack creation and before a swap, and warns about missing entries.
options.consequence: Smallest v1, but does not meet "must be preserved" literally; the backup may be told to use a skill it cannot load.

options.label: Copy the safe subset at creation, with a Sync button
options.description: Copy skills, commands and MCP server definitions (never credentials, OAuth tokens, hooks or permissions) from the primary into each backup; backup-local wins on conflict; a "Sync from primary" button in Settings re-runs it.
options.consequence: Inspectable and revocable, and the common case works. A new MCP server on the primary reaches the backup only when the user syncs or when the pre-swap check warns.

options.label: Merge the primary's config at every spawn
options.description: Pass the primary's MCP config and skill/plugin dirs into each backup's launch (Claude `--mcp-config`, ACP `mcpServers`, codex `-c`), without copying.
options.consequence: Always current, but per-kind launch plumbing and harder to inspect; a primary change takes effect on the next turn with no review.

options.label: Mirror everything, including settings and hooks
options.description: Copy the full user-level config, including `settings.json` hooks, permissions and CLI settings.
options.consequence: Most faithful, but hooks execute code and permissions change the safety posture; this needs a security review and is a much larger feature.

recommendation.reason: It makes the backup usable without copying credentials, stays inspectable, and keeps the security-sensitive hooks/permissions out of scope.

questions.title: Should Agetor ever copy or share authentication tokens between accounts?
questions.why: Copying `.credentials.json`, `auth.json`, `cli-config.json` or OpenCode's credential tables breaks the isolation model, may violate provider terms, and puts one account's token in another account's agent-writable home. This is a trust boundary, not a convenience setting.
questions.context: The investigation's assumption is no credential copying; each member must already be logged in. A related leak exists today: provider API keys in Agetor's process env (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, …) are inherited by every harness unless the harness overrides them, because `childEnv` only scrubs `AGETOR_API_TOKEN`. A "backup account" can therefore silently use the primary's key.

evidence.label: only the master token is scrubbed
alias credentials are a plain file; the built-in is the keychain

options.label: Each member uses its own login
options.description: Agetor never copies tokens. A logged-out member is skipped with a clear message; the user logs it in through the existing harness login flow.
options.consequence: Keeps the current isolation model and provider terms. The backup must be set up once, which is the honest cost of a backup account.

options.label: Copy credential files between homes
options.description: Copy the primary's token blob into the backup's home so the backup can run without its own login.
options.consequence: Rejected without a security review: a planted or stale token crosses accounts, and provider terms may forbid it.

options.label: Share a keychain item by reference
options.description: Point the backup at the primary's keychain item.
options.consequence: Only works for the built-in Claude account; not portable to alias homes or other kinds, and still shares one identity.

recommendation.reason: A backup account is a separate login by definition; copying tokens would turn a failover feature into a credential-sharing feature.

sections.title: What happens when the train runs out
sections.intro: A stack is only useful if the user knows what happens when every member is exhausted.

questions.title: When every member is exhausted, what should the task do?
questions.why: This is the difference between a short pause and a task that looks dead. It also decides whether Agetor needs persisted timers and a boot reconcile.
questions.context: The closest precedent is fx auto-resume: `Task.fxRecovery` is persisted, a timer fires, the cap is 3, and the UI shows a resume affordance. Quota resets usually have a known time (`resetsAtMs`), so Agetor can wait for the earliest one instead of polling blindly.

evidence.label: fx recovery is persisted and capped
the cap

options.label: Block with a countdown, then retry automatically
options.description: Show "all accounts exhausted — earliest reset at HH:MM", persist the intent, and retry at the earliest reset (cap 3). If it fails again, leave it blocked for a manual Run.
options.consequence: Most seamless; needs a persisted timer and boot reconcile, but the pattern already exists for fx.

options.label: Block and wait for a manual Run
options.description: Show the notice with the reset time and leave the task blocked.
options.consequence: Simplest and predictable; the user must come back and click.

options.label: Keep the task running and wait silently
options.description: Stay in `running` until a member resets.
options.consequence: Looks seamless but hides a multi-hour stall; the user cannot tell whether the agent is working.

recommendation.reason: It keeps the promise without hiding the stall, and the fx auto-resume precedent already has the persisted-state and cap mechanics to copy.

sections.title: Confirm or override
sections.intro: Defaults I would bet on. Confirm with one click, or override with what it should be.

questions.title: Name in the UI and docs

recommendation.value: **Harness stack**, with **accounts** as members and **stack** as the verb
recommendation.reason: The repo already uses "harness" for the account row and "agent" for the profile; "stack" is unambiguous and matches the requirement's language.
Enough for several plans and a backup-of-a-backup; keeps the picker and the swap UI readable.

questions.title: What the task shows during the swap

recommendation.value: The task stays `running`; the old run's failure toast is suppressed; a status line says `Switching to backup…` before the new run starts, then the swap notice
recommendation.reason: A failed toast would contradict "seamless", and a short status line explains the gap between the two processes.

recommendation.value: Persist the swap intent (like `fxRecovery`) and reconcile it on boot, so a core restart mid-swap resumes or fails cleanly
recommendation.reason: The desktop app and a headless core can hand the API port over mid-turn; an in-memory-only swap would leave a `running` task with no live run.

recommendation.value: An e2e two-account Claude stack survives a simulated limit, shows the swap notice, and preserves the conversation; per-kind adapter tests for Codex and OpenCode; a unit test for the limit classifier; and no credential file is ever copied
recommendation.reason: This is the smallest set that proves the promise rather than just the plumbing.
